name: Design a Secrets Management Service
intent: Store passwords, keys and certificates for thousands of workloads so that a stolen disk, a stolen token or a single leaked secret does not hand over everything, and so that every read can be traced.
codeTitle: a vault with key shares, envelope encryption and leases
finalIntro: A billing workload asking for a database password and getting one that expires.
prompt: Design a secrets management service in the style of HashiCorp Vault or a cloud key management service. About 2,000 workloads need database passwords, API keys and certificates. Secrets must be encrypted at rest, only the workloads that need them may read them, every read must be recorded, secrets must be rotated, the service must stay up when a machine or a region fails, and a leaked secret must do as little harm as possible.
functional: Store and read secrets by path, with versions
Authenticate machines and people, and hand out short-lived tokens
Allow or deny each request by policy
Create database credentials on demand, with a lease that expires and is revoked
Rotate secrets and encryption keys without downtime
Record every request, allowed or denied, in an audit log
Offer a break-glass path for emergencies
nonFunctional: Secrets are never stored in plain text, and a stolen disk or backup reveals nothing
A read takes under 20 ms, and the service handles tens of thousands of reads per second with client caching
Available when a node or a whole zone fails, with no loss of acknowledged writes
If the audit log cannot be written, requests are refused
One compromised workload or token exposes only what its policy allows
The master key never exists in one person's hands or in plain text on disk

firstAttempt.text: Put the secrets in environment variables and config files in the deployment repository, with one shared database password for every service, encrypted with one key kept next to the files. Rotating means editing the files and redeploying everything.
limits: Anyone who can read the repository or a backup can read every secret
One shared password means one leak exposes every system, and nobody knows which service used it
Rotation needs a coordinated redeploy of every service, so it is postponed for years
There is no record of who read what, and no way to cut off one workload
The key that encrypts the files is stored beside them

steps.title: Encrypt every secret under its own data key
steps.problem: A database or a backup that holds secrets in plain text turns any disk theft, snapshot leak or careless administrator into a total breach, and a single key for everything is a single point of failure that is impossible to rotate.
steps.fix: Put an API in front of an encrypted store and use envelope encryption. Each secret is encrypted with its own random data encryption key (DEK). Each DEK is itself encrypted ('wrapped') by a key encryption key higher up, and that key by the master key. The store holds only ciphertext and wrapped DEKs. To read a secret the service unwraps its DEK in memory, decrypts, returns the value over TLS and forgets the key. The ciphers are authenticated (AES-GCM) with the secret's path as associated data (extra text the cipher checks but does not hide), so a ciphertext copied to another path fails to decrypt.
steps.tradeoff: A stolen disk reveals nothing, and rotating a key higher in the hierarchy means rewrapping small DEKs instead of re-encrypting all data. Every read now does a key unwrap, and the whole design rests on the master key, which has to live somewhere safe, which is the next problem.

steps.title: Protect the master key: HSM and Shamir shares
steps.problem: The service must hold the master key to work, but a key on the same disk as the data, or one that a single administrator can copy, defeats the encryption.
steps.fix: The master key is generated and kept inside a hardware security module (HSM), or a cloud key service backed by one, which performs wrap and unwrap and never lets the key out. When no HSM is available the vault uses Shamir secret sharing: the master key is split into 5 shares such that any 3 recreate it and any 2 reveal nothing, and the shares go to five different people. On start-up the service is sealed and holds no key in memory. It serves nothing until three share holders unseal it, or until the HSM auto-unseals it with an identity check. A sealed vault can also be locked again on purpose in seconds.
steps.tradeoff: No single person or disk can decrypt the data, and a break-in at the disk gives nothing. A restart needs people or an HSM before service resumes, auto-unseal makes the cloud key service a dependency of recovery, and losing three of the five shares loses the data for good.

steps.title: Prove who the workload is, then check a policy for every request
steps.problem: A password that every service knows says nothing about who is asking, so you cannot give the billing service its own secrets and keep the marketing site out of them, or tell afterwards who read what.
steps.fix: Workloads prove their identity with something the platform vouches for, such as a Kubernetes service account token or a cloud instance identity document, which the vault verifies against the platform. It returns a short-lived token, valid for 15 minutes, tied to a policy: a list of paths and the actions allowed on each, denied by default. Every request is checked against that policy, and every request, allowed or denied, writes an audit entry (who, path, time, result, with secret values hashed) before the answer is sent. If no audit device can be written, the request is refused.
steps.tradeoff: Each workload sees only its own paths, a stolen token expires within minutes, and the audit log answers who read the secret. Policies need careful maintenance, the identity provider becomes a dependency, and a log that blocks requests when it is full is a deliberate choice of safety over availability.

steps.title: Generate dynamic secrets with leases
steps.problem: A stored database password is the same for everyone and valid for years, so a leak is both wide and long, and rotating it breaks every system that holds a copy.
steps.fix: An engine creates credentials on demand. When billing asks for database access, the vault connects to the database with a privileged account and runs CREATE ROLE with a random name and password, with the grants the policy allows, and returns it with a lease: an id and a time to live of one hour. The workload renews the lease while it needs it, up to a maximum. When the lease expires, or an operator revokes it, the vault drops the role. Revoking a whole role or path revokes every lease below it at once.
steps.tradeoff: A leaked credential belongs to one workload and dies by itself within the hour, nothing static is left to rotate, and each credential names the workload that used it. The vault is now on the path to the database, it holds a privileged database account, and it must track every lease and clean up roles that it failed to drop.

steps.title: Make it highly available with Raft and cache on the clients
steps.problem: Every workload depends on the vault, so a single node is a single point of failure for the whole company, and reading a secret on every request would put 100,000 reads per second on it.
steps.fix: Run 5 vault nodes with an integrated Raft log as the storage (Raft is a protocol that makes nodes agree on one ordered log): one leader accepts writes and replicates them, and a write is acknowledged once 3 of 5 nodes have it, so any 2 nodes can fail without losing an acknowledged write. If the leader dies, the others elect a new one in seconds. Standbys forward writes to the leader, and some can serve reads. On the workload side an agent logs in once, caches secrets and leases, renews them in the background at about two thirds of their life, and serves the application from memory. The fleet then makes about one read per secret per lease instead of one per request.
steps.tradeoff: The service survives a node or a zone, and read load falls by orders of magnitude. All writes go through one leader, which limits write throughput. Cached copies are not individually audited and can outlive a revocation until the next refresh, so cache lifetimes are kept short.

steps.title: Replicate across regions, limit the blast radius, keep a break-glass path
steps.problem: A whole region can fail, a compromised administrator or token can try to reach everything, and the one time everything is broken is the time the vault must still be reachable.
steps.fix: A second cluster in another region follows the first with asynchronous replication and takes over in a disaster. Some data, such as dynamic engines and tokens, can stay local to each region so that a regional failure or a leak stays regional. Separate namespaces and mounts per team keep policy mistakes contained, the root token is revoked after the first setup, and administration is done with short-lived tokens. The break-glass path is a documented procedure: several people combine key shares or approve a time-boxed emergency token, every step is audited, and an alert fires the moment it is used, followed by a rotation of what it touched.
steps.tradeoff: A regional disaster is survivable, and one mistake reaches a small part of the system. Asynchronous replication can lose the last few writes on failover, a promotion needs a decision, and break-glass access is powerful, so it needs more care than any other part of the design.

failures.scenario: The leader node dies during a write
failures.impact: A client may not know whether its write happened, and the vault is briefly without a leader.
failures.answer: A write is acknowledged only after a majority has it, so the remaining 4 nodes elect a new leader within a few seconds and it has every acknowledged write. Clients retry with backoff. A write that was not acknowledged either exists everywhere or nowhere, and retried writes are safe because setting a secret to a value is idempotent.

failures.scenario: The vault restarts and comes up sealed
failures.impact: No workload can read anything, and new database credentials cannot be created.
failures.answer: Workloads keep running on their cached secrets and existing leases while the vault is sealed, which is why leases are longer than the longest expected unseal time. Auto-unseal through the HSM restores service in a minute, or three share holders unseal by hand. The on-call is paged as soon as the node reports sealed.

failures.impact: The thief can read everything in that workload's policy.
failures.answer: The token expires within 15 minutes and can only reach the paths in its policy. The audit log shows reads from an unexpected address, an alert fires, and the token and its leases are revoked together, which drops the dynamic database roles too. Because credentials were dynamic, nothing static needs rotating.

failures.scenario: The database is down when leases expire or when the vault tries to revoke
failures.impact: Expired roles stay in the database, and new credentials cannot be created.
failures.answer: Revocation is queued and retried with backoff until the role is dropped, and a periodic sweep compares the lease table with the roles that exist. Roles also carry a database-side expiry date as a second line of defence. Callers get a clear error rather than a stale credential.

failures.scenario: The audit log device is full or unreachable
failures.impact: If requests continue without a record, reads become untraceable.
failures.answer: The vault refuses requests when no audit device accepts the entry, since an unrecorded read is worse than a failed one. Several audit devices run at once, so one failure changes nothing, and disk usage alerts fire well before the log is full.

alternatives.title: Where the master key lives

options.name: Shamir shares held by people
options.pro: No cloud dependency, and no single person can decrypt
options.con: Every restart needs people, which is slow at 3 a.m.

options.name: Auto-unseal with a cloud key service or HSM
options.con: The cloud key service becomes a dependency of recovery, and whoever controls it controls the vault

options.name: Key in a config file
options.con: No protection: the key sits beside the data

alternatives.pick: HSM or cloud key auto-unseal for daily operation, with Shamir recovery shares kept for the case where that service is gone.

alternatives.title: Static secrets or dynamic secrets

options.name: Static secrets with scheduled rotation
options.pro: Works with anything that takes a password
options.con: Every consumer must reload, so rotation is risky and rare, and a leak lasts until the next rotation

options.name: Dynamic secrets with leases
options.pro: Unique per workload, short-lived and revoked automatically
options.con: The vault needs a privileged account and must be available, and the target system must support creating credentials

alternatives.pick: Dynamic wherever the target supports it, static with automated rotation for the rest.

alternatives.title: Read through the vault or cache on the client

options.name: Read on every use
options.pro: Instant revocation and a complete audit trail
options.con: The vault sees every request and becomes the bottleneck

options.name: Agent that caches and renews
options.pro: Orders of magnitude fewer reads, and workloads survive short vault outages
options.con: Revocation takes effect at the next refresh, and cached reads are not audited

alternatives.pick: Agent caching with short leases, and direct reads only for the most sensitive secrets.

alternatives.title: How the storage is replicated

options.name: Integrated Raft
options.pro: No second system to run, and strong consistency within a cluster
options.con: Write throughput is limited to what one leader does

options.name: External store such as Consul or a SQL database
options.con: One more system to secure and keep available, and it sits on the critical path

alternatives.pick: Integrated Raft, with asynchronous replication to a second region.

roles.label: Callers
roles.description: Workloads and the people who use break-glass.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The vault API and the client-side agent cache.

roles.label: Control
roles.description: Identity, policy, key handling and lease engines.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The encrypted store, the HSM, the Raft log and the target database.

quiz.question: A vault stores 10 million secrets, all encrypted with one key. Security asks for the key to be rotated every quarter, but re-encrypting 10 million secrets takes days and risks outages. Which design makes rotation cheap?
options: Encrypt the whole database volume with a single disk key, and rotate that key by re-encrypting the entire volume in place
Keep the single key in an environment variable of the vault process so that it can be replaced by a rolling restart
Store a salted hash of each secret instead of the ciphertext, so no key exists to rotate
Give each secret its own data key, wrap those with a key encryption key, and rotate by rewrapping the small keys
quiz.explanation: With envelope encryption, rotating a higher key means rewrapping small data keys, not re-encrypting the secrets themselves. A volume key still means re-encrypting everything on rotation and gives no protection once the volume is mounted. A hash cannot be reversed, so workloads could never read the secret back.

quiz.question: Assume 2,000 workloads use 20 secrets each, so 40,000 secrets, and agents cache them and renew at two thirds of a 1-hour lease. The payments team needs a revoked secret to stop working within about 5 minutes. Their 500 secrets are the only ones with that need. What is the best approach?
options: Turn off agent caching for the whole fleet so every revocation is instant, accepting about 100,000 reads per second on the vault
Keep 1-hour leases and add 10 Raft nodes so direct reads for all workloads become affordable
Give only the payments secrets a lease of about 6 minutes, renewed every 4, costing about 2 vault reads per second
Keep 1-hour leases, since renewal at two thirds of the lease revokes a secret within 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: Lease length is the knob for revocation delay, and a short lease on 500 secrets is only 500 / 240 s, about 2 reads per second. Removing caching moves the whole read load to the vault. More Raft nodes make every write wait for a bigger majority and would pay for 100,000 reads per second to serve a need that only 500 secrets have, and a 1-hour lease can leave a revoked secret in a cache for about 40 minutes.

quiz.question: The vault's single audit device, a local disk, fills up at 2 a.m. and the vault now refuses every request, so workloads cannot read their secrets. An engineer wants to keep serving requests without audit entries until morning. What is the best design response?
options: Switch to fail-open: keep serving, and buffer the audit entries in memory to write out once the disk has been cleared
Keep refusing when no audit device accepts the entry, but run several audit devices and alert on disk use early
Keep serving reads of existing secrets and refuse only writes, since writes are the operations that change the state of the system
Stop writing audit entries for denied requests, which are most of the volume and never return a secret
quiz.explanation: An unrecorded secret read is worse than a failed one, so the design stays closed. Redundant audit devices and early alerts remove the single point of failure. An in-memory buffer loses entries on a crash, reads are exactly the events that need recording, and denied requests are among the most useful entries for spotting an attack.
